title: The business case as the project's baseline
blurb: Explain why the business case is the project's baseline and why every significant change must be checked against it.
question: A logistics firm is halfway through deploying warehouse robots. A key supplier raises its prices by 30% and the expected labour savings are revised down. The project manager says: 'The plan is approved, so we just carry on.' Why is that wrong, and what should happen next?

teach.body: A business case is the justification for the initiation, investment and/or continuation of a project, set out in terms of benefits, costs and risks. In plain English, it answers two questions: why are we doing this, and is it still worth doing? The sponsor owns it and the project manager provides input. It is approved before serious money is committed, and it stays live for the whole project.

teach.h: What a business case weighs up
teach.caption: Benefits must outweigh costs and risks, and the project must fit the organisation's strategy. Change any of these and the balance can tip.

teach.h: Why it is the project's baseline
teach.body: A baseline is the agreed reference point you measure against. The business case is the project's most fundamental one: scope, schedule, budget and quality all exist to deliver its justification. The project management plan says HOW the work will be done; the business case says WHY it is worth doing. So when anything significant changes, the first test is not 'can we still deliver the plan?' but 'is the project still justified?'

teach.h: The business case through a linear life cycle

steps.label: Concept
steps.sub: Sponsor drafts the case; options compared

steps.label: Definition
steps.sub: Case refined with firmer costs; approved at the gate

steps.label: Deployment
steps.sub: Re-checked at each gate and for every major change

steps.label: Transition
steps.sub: Benefits handed to owners in the business

steps.label:
Benefits
realisation
steps.sub: Benefits reviews measure results against the case

teach.caption: The case is not written once and filed. It is revisited at every decision gate, and it outlives the project into benefits realisation.

teach.h: Changes that can undermine the case
head: Change
Why it matters
rows: More or less is delivered, so benefits and costs shift
Higher spend may wipe out the net benefit
Late delivery delays or shrinks benefits
New threats lower the chance of success
Forecasts revised down weaken the justification
teach.caption: Any SIGNIFICANT change in these areas must be assessed against the business case, not just against the schedule.

teach.h: After a review: three possible outcomes

root.label: Does the case still hold?
root.sub: Reviewed at a gate or when a change is proposed

children.label: Continue
children.sub: Update the baseline through change control

children.label: Re-plan
children.sub: Rescope or rethink so it is justified again

children.label: Close early
children.sub: Stop in a controlled way; capture lessons

teach.caption: Closing a project that is no longer justified is governance working, not failing. Money already spent is not a reason to keep spending.

teach.h: Reviewing the case: linear vs iterative

rows.label: When reviewed
values: Lighter, more frequent: per release or time box

rows.label: What usually flexes
values: Time and cost, through change control

rows.label: Who protects value
values: Product owner each iteration, sponsor overall

rows.label: Formal re-check if
values: Any significant change to the baseline
Fixed time, cost or objectives must change

teach.caption: Both life cycles keep the case at the centre. Iterative projects protect it by delivering the highest-value items first within fixed time and cost.

teach.body: The case promised £1.2m a year in labour savings for £3m. In Deployment, the robot supplier raises prices by 30% and a pilot shows savings nearer £0.8m. The project manager raises a change, assesses the impact and reports to the sponsor. The board re-checks the case: payback has stretched from three to five years. It decides to re-plan, automating two aisles instead of four, which restores an acceptable return.

teach.text: Two classic traps. 1) The PROJECT MANAGER does not own the business case: the SPONSOR does, with the PM providing input. 2) An approved business case is not 'done'. Options saying it is fixed once approved, reviewed only at closure, or replaced by the project management plan are wrong. It is reviewed regularly, especially at decision gates.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define it: the justification for the project in terms of benefits, costs and risks, owned by the sponsor.
Explain why it is the baseline: every decision about scope, time and cost is measured against that justification.
Say when it is reviewed: regularly, at every decision gate, and whenever a significant change is proposed.
Give the consequence: if it no longer holds, re-plan or close the project rather than keep spending.
Add a short example, such as a cost rise that stretches payback beyond what the board will accept.
Business case: justification for initiating, investing in and continuing a project (benefits vs costs and risks).
Owned by the sponsor; the project manager provides input and flags changes that affect it.
It is the project's baseline: the reference all significant decisions are measured against.
Review it regularly, especially at decision gates and whenever scope, cost, time, risk, benefits or the environment change.
If it no longer holds: re-plan or close. Sunk cost is not a reason to continue.

summary: You can now explain what a business case is and why it forms the project's baseline. You can also explain why the impact of every significant change must be assessed against it, and what should happen when it no longer holds.

A.q: Who owns the business case for a project?
options: The project manager
The project sponsor
The project office
The steering group
A.why: The sponsor owns the business case and is accountable for the benefits it promises. The project manager provides input.

whyNot.0: The project manager contributes to the business case and flags changes, but does not own it.
whyNot.2: A project office may support with templates and assurance, but it does not own the justification.
whyNot.3: The steering group or board reviews the case at gates; ownership sits with the sponsor, who usually chairs it.

A.q: Which statement BEST explains why the business case is described as the baseline for a project?
options: It fixes the budget so it cannot be changed
It is the detailed schedule the team follows
It is what every key decision is tested against
It lists every requirement users have asked for
A.why: A baseline is the agreed reference point. The business case's justification is what scope, time, cost and every major decision are measured against.

whyNot.0: Budgets can change through change control; what matters is whether the case still justifies the project.
whyNot.1: The schedule is part of the project management plan, which says how, not why.
whyNot.3: Requirements are managed through requirements management; the business case justifies the investment.

A.q: A council's library refurbishment uncovers asbestos, adding 20% to the cost. What should happen FIRST in relation to the business case?
options: Absorb the cost quietly to protect the end date
Close the project at once to stop further spend
Insist the contractor carries all the extra cost
Assess whether the case is still justified
A.why: A significant cost change must be assessed against the business case so the sponsor can decide whether to continue, re-plan or close.

whyNot.0: Hiding a significant change bypasses governance and may mean spending on a project that is no longer justified.
whyNot.1: Closing may be the right outcome, but only after the impact on the case has been assessed.
whyNot.2: Who pays depends on the contract; the first step is to understand the impact on the justification.

B.q:
Which TWO of the following would be reasons to review a project's business case?
1) A major supplier raises its prices
2) The weekly team meeting moves to Tuesdays
3) A new regulation reduces the expected benefits
4) A team member takes planned annual leave
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Price rises and regulatory changes affect costs and benefits, so both can change whether the project is justified.

whyNot.0: Moving a team meeting has no effect on benefits, costs or risks.
whyNot.2: Neither a meeting change nor planned leave is a significant change to the justification.
whyNot.3: A regulation change matters, but planned leave is normal resource management, not a business case trigger.

B.q: Complete the statement: a business case justifies a project in terms of its ___.
options: benefits, costs and risks
scope, time and quality
stakeholders and roles
outputs and work packages
B.why: The business case weighs the benefits against the costs and risks to justify initiating, investing in and continuing the project.

whyNot.1: Scope, time and quality are delivery constraints planned in the project management plan.
whyNot.2: Stakeholders and roles are covered by stakeholder analysis and governance, not the justification.
whyNot.3: Outputs and work packages describe what is built and how work is broken down (PBS and WBS).

B.q: An insurer is building a claims app iteratively, with a fixed budget and fixed release date. Users ask for a large new feature. How is the business case MOST likely protected?
options: The release date moves back to fit it in
The budget is increased to pay for it
The product owner reprioritises the backlog
The sponsor rewrites the case every time box
B.why: In iterative working time and cost are fixed, so the product owner reprioritises scope to keep the highest-value items, protecting the justification.

whyNot.0: Moving fixed dates is not the iterative norm; scope flexes instead.
whyNot.1: Cost is fixed; raising it would need a formal re-check of the case, not be the default.
whyNot.3: The case is checked more lightly and frequently in iterative work, but it is not rewritten every time box.

C.q: Halfway through Deployment, a retailer learns a competitor has opened next to its planned new store, halving forecast sales. Costs are unchanged. What is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Re-assess the case, then re-plan or close
Continue as costs have not changed at all
Speed up delivery to open before the rival
Log it as a team issue and keep reporting
C.why: Halving the benefits is a significant change to the external environment and the business case must be re-assessed. If it no longer holds, the project is re-planned or closed.

whyNot.1: A project can lose its justification through falling benefits even when costs hold steady.
whyNot.2: Speeding up adds cost and risk and doesn't answer whether the project is still worth doing.
whyNot.3: This affects the justification itself, so it must go to the sponsor, not stay with the team.

C.q: Which is NOT a likely consequence of failing to review the business case when significant changes occur?
options: Money keeps flowing to a project that no longer pays back
Benefit forecasts drift away from what is now realistic
Gates approve work against out-of-date assumptions
The sponsor gains clearer accountability for benefits
C.why: Failing to review the case weakens control. It does not make accountability clearer; if anything it blurs it.

whyNot.0: Without a review, a project can keep spending after it has stopped being worth it.
whyNot.1: Unreviewed forecasts become stale and misleading.
whyNot.2: Decision gates rely on a current case; an old one means decisions on false assumptions.

C.q: A project manager says: 'The business case was approved at the start, so my job now is just to deliver the plan.' Which response BEST corrects this?
options: The case is replaced by the plan once approved
The case is only looked at after handover
The case is the PM's to rewrite as needed
The case must be re-checked as things change
C.why: The business case is a live baseline. Changes must be assessed against it, and the PM should flag anything that threatens it to the sponsor.

whyNot.0: The plan says how the work is done; it never replaces the justification for doing it.
whyNot.1: Reviewing only after handover would be too late to change course.
whyNot.2: The sponsor owns the case; the PM provides input rather than rewriting it.

reteach.title: A house extension that stops making sense
reteach.question: You are building a kitchen extension to add £40,000 of value to your home for £30,000. Halfway through, the builder finds the ground needs £25,000 of piling. What does your 'business case' tell you to do?

blocks.h: The reason you started is the yardstick
blocks.body: Your reason for building was simple: spend £30,000, gain £40,000 of value and more space. That is your business case, and it is your baseline. The piling news doesn't just change the budget; it changes whether the extension is still worth it. Spending £55,000 for £40,000 of value only makes sense if the extra space is worth the difference to you. So you stop, re-check, and decide: carry on, shrink the design, or stop.

blocks.text: 'We've already spent £15,000, so we must finish' is the sunk-cost trap. The business case looks at what is still to come: remaining costs against remaining benefits.

explain.body: The justification for initiating, investing in and continuing a project, in terms of benefits, costs and risks. The sponsor owns it; the project manager provides input.

items.label: the benefits the project will bring

test.q: What is the main purpose of a project's business case?
options: To set out the detailed team schedule
To allocate work packages to the team
To justify investing in the project
To record lessons for future projects
test.why: The business case justifies the investment by weighing benefits against costs and risks.

whyNot.0: The schedule sits in the project management plan.
whyNot.1: Work packages come from the WBS and are allocated through the OBS and RACI.
whyNot.3: Lessons are captured in reviews and lessons logs, not the business case.

explain.body: Because the project exists to deliver its justification, the business case is the reference point every significant decision is measured against. The plan explains how; the case explains why.

test.q: A board compares a proposed scope change against the business case before deciding. What does this show?
options: The case is acting as the baseline
The case has replaced the change log
The board manages daily delivery
The case is now the quality plan
test.why: Testing changes against the justification is exactly what it means for the business case to be the project's baseline.

whyNot.1: Changes are still logged in the change log; the case is what they are assessed against.
whyNot.2: The board directs and decides; the PM manages day-to-day delivery.
whyNot.3: Quality planning is separate, though quality indicators trace back to the case.

explain.body: Regularly through the life cycle: at every decision gate, and whenever a significant change to scope, cost, time, risk, benefits or the external environment is proposed or occurs.

test.q: When should a project's business case be reviewed?
options: Only when the budget has been overspent
Regularly, especially at decision gates
Once only, when the project is approved
Only at the final post-project review
test.why: The case is reviewed regularly, especially at decision gates and when significant changes occur.

whyNot.0: Overspend is one trigger, but falling benefits or new risks matter just as much.
whyNot.2: A single review at approval leaves the project running on stale assumptions.
whyNot.3: By the post-project review it is too late to change course.

explain.body: Continue (update the baseline through change control), re-plan (rescope so it is justified again), or close the project early in a controlled way. Spend already incurred doesn't count in favour of continuing.

test.q: A gate review finds the remaining benefits now fall well short of the remaining costs, with no way to recover them. What should the sponsor recommend?
options: Continue as planned to avoid wasted spend
Appoint a new PM and keep going
Cut testing to bring the costs down
Close the project in a controlled way
test.why: If the case can no longer be justified, the project should be closed in a controlled way, capturing lessons.

whyNot.0: That is the sunk-cost trap: only future costs and benefits matter.
whyNot.1: A new PM doesn't fix a project whose justification has gone.
whyNot.2: Cutting testing risks quality and still doesn't restore the case.
